text: Reteaming is hard. Reorgs are hard. You can't lump them all into one thing with oh, it's all great all the time. No, it's not.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: At the opening of the podcast, Heidi sets the foundation for why organizational change and team restructuring matters. She acknowledges that while the ultimate goal is building great products and achieving product-market fit, there's an additional complexity layer that many companies overlook - the human element of how teams are organized and how they change over time.
text_ko: 팀 재구성(reteaming)은 힘들어요. 조직 개편(reorgs)도 마찬가지예요. 이걸 다 한데 묶어서 '아, 항상 다 괜찮아요' 식으로 말하면 안 돼요. 절대 그렇지 않아요.
text_zh: 重新组队很难搞，重组也很难搞。你不能把这些都混在一起说"哎呀，这些都很棒，随时都很棒"。才不是呢。
text_es: Reorganizar equipos es complicado. Las reestructuraciones son complicadas. No puedes meter todo en el mismo saco y decir "ay, todo está genial siempre". No, no es así.
key_sentence: Reteaming is hard. Reorgs are hard.
original_text: Reteaming is hard. Reorgs are hard. You can't lump them all into one thing with oh, it's all great all the time. No, it's not. If we could just build the software, deliver to the customer, get the product market fit, hey, have we delighted them or not? If only it could be that easy. No, we have the people layer, so let's focus there too.

text: I think a lot of the things that I would read about teams just are naturally focused on, well, you want to build things that customers love. You want it to be an enjoyable experience, you want to deliver on time.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: Lenny asks Heidi to elaborate on the 'people layer' concept she mentioned earlier. Heidi explains that while most business advice focuses on product delivery and customer satisfaction, there's an equally important but often overlooked aspect of company building - designing and managing the human structures and team organizations as companies scale from small startups to large organizations.
text_ko: 제가 팀에 관해 읽어본 글들은 대부분 자연스럽게 '고객이 좋아할 걸 만들어야 한다', '사용자에게 즐거운 경험을 줘야 한다', '약속한 기한에 맞춰 전달해야 한다' 같은 데 초점이 맞춰져 있더라고요.
text_zh: 我觉得很多关于团队的文章都会很自然地聚焦在这些点上：你得做出客户真正喜欢的产品，用户体验要好，还得按时交付。
text_es: Creo que muchas de las cosas que leía sobre equipos se enfocan naturalmente en, bueno, quieres crear cosas que los clientes realmente amen. Quieres que sea una experiencia que disfruten, quieres cumplir con los tiempos de entrega.
key_sentence: you want to build things that customers love.
original_text: I think a lot of the things that I would read about teams just are naturally focused on, well, you want to build things that customers love. You want it to be an enjoyable experience, you want to deliver on time. There's a reason we're there as a business, but there's also a lot of company building that happens in building the people structures and just when you go from one to many to a multitude, there's a lot of work that goes into it.

vocabulary.definition: To complete and provide a product or service by the agreed-upon deadline.
vocabulary.businessContext: Timely delivery is essential in business operations, as it affects project timelines, customer trust, and overall service quality.
vocabulary.nuance: While delivering on time is crucial, it should not compromise the quality of the product or service being delivered.

vocabulary.definition: A positive and pleasurable interaction that a customer has with a product, service, or brand.
vocabulary.businessContext: Creating an enjoyable experience is vital in customer service and product design, as it can lead to increased customer loyalty and positive word-of-mouth.
vocabulary.nuance: The term emphasizes the emotional aspect of customer interactions, suggesting that enjoyment can enhance overall satisfaction.

vocabulary.definition: To create or develop products, services, or solutions, often involving design and engineering processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, 'building things' refers to the iterative process of developing prototypes, software, or physical products to meet market needs.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase can imply a hands-on, creative approach to problem-solving, often associated with innovation and entrepreneurship.

text: So we rolled these whiteboards out and it had the team structure with everyone's names on it.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: Lenny asks about how to take advantage of reorg opportunities for career advancement. Heidi shares a story about transparent reorganization at Procore, where they used 'whiteboard reteaming' - a method inspired by Spotify where leadership visualized the new team structure on whiteboards and invited all 80 affected employees to provide input and express interest in different roles before finalizing the changes.
text_ko: 그래서 저희는 이 화이트보드를 도입했는데, 그 위에 팀 구성도와 팀원들 이름이 적혀 있었어요.
text_zh: 所以我们就把这些白板推出来了，上面画着团队架构，每个人的名字都在上面。
text_es: Entonces desplegamos estas pizarras y tenían la estructura del equipo con los nombres de todos.
key_sentence: it had the team structure with everyone's names on it.
original_text: So we rolled these whiteboards out and it had the team structure with everyone's names on it. It had the name of the team, the mission of the team, how many open slots for hiring across all of these different teams, and then people's names in their existing team positions. And people were invited to look, give feedback. They identified mistakes that we had in the design, 'Oh, this team might be better over here and here's why.' And people had the opportunity to see opportunities within their own company that they might say, 'Hey, I'm interested in this, might I be considered for this?'

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of roles, responsibilities, and relationships within a team, defining how tasks are coordinated and executed.
vocabulary.businessContext: A well-defined team structure is crucial in business settings to enhance collaboration, clarify reporting lines, and improve overall productivity.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a hierarchy or a flat organization, and the choice of structure should align with the team's goals and culture.

text: There's another framework that I really like. I don't think it's in my book, but I've written about it in my new book, but it's called RIDE. And we had a chief people officer at Procore and she's now at UKG, Pat Wadors.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: Lenny asks about how to manage the complexity of involving teams in reorganization decisions. Heidi introduces the RIDE framework (Request, Input, Decide, Execute) created by Pat Wadors, which clarifies roles and responsibilities in organizational changes. This framework helps avoid confusion about who has decision-making authority versus who can provide input during team restructuring processes.
text_ko: 제가 정말 좋아하는 다른 프레임워크 (framework)가 하나 있어요. 제 책에는 없는 것 같은데 새 책에서는 다뤘어요. RIDE라고 불러요. Procore에서 최고 인사 책임자 (chief people officer)로 계셨고 지금은 UKG에 계신 Pat Wadors예요.
text_zh: 还有一个框架我特别喜欢。我记得之前那本书里没写，但新书里有提到，叫做RIDE框架。这是我们Procore的首席人事官Pat Wadors提出的，她现在在UKG工作。
text_es: Hay otro modelo que me gusta mucho. No creo que esté en mi libro, pero sí lo incluí en el nuevo, y se llama RIDE. Tuvimos una directora de recursos humanos (chief people officer) en Procore y ahora está en UKG, Pat Wadors.
original_text: There's another framework that I really like. I don't think it's in my book, but I've written about it in my new book, but it's called RIDE. And we had a chief people officer at Procore and she's now at UKG, Pat Wadors. She taught us the RIDE framework for decision making clarity and it's who's requesting the change, who can give input to the change, who's the decider on the change, and who's going to execute on the change?

vocabulary.definition: A framework is a structured system or set of guidelines that provides a foundation for developing or organizing ideas, processes, or projects.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, frameworks are often used to standardize practices, enhance collaboration, and streamline project management, such as in software development or strategic planning.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'framework' suggests a supportive structure, it can also imply rigidity; therefore, it is important to ensure flexibility within the framework to adapt to changing circumstances.

text: So taking a team off to the side, giving that team process freedom. They didn't want us distracted from the drag. When you're working on an existing product line, you get this cadence and it can become a mature cadence.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: Heidi shares the story of how Expertcity (which became GoTo products) successfully pivoted by using an 'isolation' reteaming pattern. When their original marketplace product failed, leadership created a small isolated team to work on GoToMyPC with complete process freedom. Heidi explains that existing product teams develop established rhythms that work for mature products, but new innovations require much faster iteration cycles.
text_ko: 그래서 팀 하나를 따로 떼어놓고 그 팀에 프로세스 자율성(process freedom)을 줬어요. 그들은 우리가 본업의 흐름에서 벗어나 산만해지는 걸 원치 않았어요. 기존 제품 라인에서 일할 때는 이런 업무 리듬(cadence)이 생기고, 그게 자리 잡으면 꽤 성숙한 리듬이 돼요.
text_zh: 所以就把团队单独拉出来，给他们流程上的自由度。他们不希望我们被那些拖后腿的事情分心。当你在做现有产品线的时候，会形成一种节奏，时间久了这个节奏就会变得很成熟。
text_es: Entonces agarrar un equipo y apartarlo, darle a ese equipo libertad de proceso. No querían que nos distrajéramos de lo que nos estaba frenando. Cuando trabajas en una línea de productos que ya existe, agarras cierto ritmo y puede convertirse en un ritmo muy establecido.
original_text: So taking a team off to the side, giving that team process freedom. They didn't want us distracted from the drag. When you're working on an existing product line, you get this cadence and it can become a mature cadence. Maybe people work in two weeks or one week now, but when you're working on something new, you need faster iteration loops. And our founders knew that need.

vocabulary.definition: The autonomy given to a team to determine their own methods and workflows in completing tasks or projects.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, particularly in startups, process freedom allows teams to innovate and adapt their approaches without excessive oversight, fostering creativity and efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: While process freedom encourages innovation, it should be balanced with accountability to ensure alignment with overall business goals.

vocabulary.definition: Having one's attention diverted from the primary task or focus, often leading to reduced productivity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business environment, being distracted can negatively impact team performance and project outcomes, making it essential to minimize interruptions.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting a lack of focus that can hinder progress.

vocabulary.definition: The rhythmic flow or pattern of activity, often referring to the regularity and timing of processes or meetings.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, establishing a cadence for meetings or product releases helps teams maintain momentum and predictability in their workflows.
vocabulary.nuance: Cadence implies a sense of routine that can enhance productivity, but it should not become so rigid that it stifles creativity.

vocabulary.definition: Having developed to a point of full functionality, stability, and reliability, often used to describe products or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a mature product line indicates that the offerings have been refined and optimized based on market feedback and performance metrics.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'mature' suggests reliability, it can also imply a lack of innovation if not balanced with ongoing development.

text: And so, one, separate location. There's another story in the book about a team that incubated a product idea within Citrix and they were in a garage of all places, so they were really isolated.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: Lenny asks about how to make isolated innovation teams successful, since the 'startup within a company' approach often fails. Heidi provides concrete advice for the isolation reteaming pattern: physically separate the team, have leadership explicitly protect them from interruptions, and ensure they have process freedom to work differently from the main organization.
text_ko: 그래서 첫째는 장소를 따로 분리하는 거예요. 책에 나오는 또 다른 이야기는 시트릭스 안에서 제품 아이디어를 인큐베이팅(incubated)하던 팀 얘기인데, 그 팀은 하필 차고에 있어서 정말 고립돼 있었어요.
text_zh: 所以说，第一点，要单独找个地方。书里还有一个故事，讲的是Citrix内部有个团队孵化产品创意，他们就在一个车库里办公，你能想象吗，完全与世隔绝的那种。
text_es: Y entonces, una ubicación separada. Hay otra historia en el libro sobre un equipo que desarrolló una idea de producto dentro de Citrix y estaban en un garaje, imagínate, así que estaban realmente aislados del resto.
original_text: And so, one, separate location. There's another story in the book about a team that incubated a product idea within Citrix and they were in a garage of all places, so they were really isolated. But just put the team in a different region, make it that area. That's number one. Number two, tell other people not to disturb this team. That's key. And hearing it from a leader is really, really important.

vocabulary.definition: To nurture and develop an idea or project in a controlled environment until it is ready for launch or further growth.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, incubation often refers to the process of supporting early-stage companies or ideas through mentorship, funding, and resources to foster innovation.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'incubated' suggests a protective and supportive environment, it may imply a lack of immediate market exposure or urgency.

vocabulary.definition: Separated from others; existing independently or apart from a larger group or system.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, isolation can refer to teams or projects that operate independently, which may lead to innovation but can also hinder collaboration and resource sharing.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'isolated' often carries a negative connotation, suggesting a lack of communication or support, which may not be ideal for team dynamics.

text: So you need to shed their skin of the other things that they're working on. If you take a bigger picture, kind of forest through the trees picture, you want people pairing and switching pairs so they're not single owners of the system.
speaker: Heidi Helfand
context: Continuing her advice on successful isolation teams, Heidi explains how companies can prepare for this type of reteaming by building knowledge redundancy. She advocates for pair programming and regular switching of pairs so that no single person becomes the sole owner of critical systems, which makes it easier for people to join special projects without leaving knowledge gaps behind.
text_ko: 그래서 그들이 맡고 있는 다른 일들을 내려놓게 해야 해요. 좀 더 큰 그림(숲을 보는 관점)에서는 사람들이 페어링(pairing)을 하고 페어를 바꿔가며(switching pairs) 일해서 누구도 시스템의 단독 소유자(single owners)가 되지 않게 하고 싶어요.
text_zh: 所以你得让他们把手头其他的事情都放一放。从大局来看，就是要让大家结对工作，而且要经常换搭档，这样就不会出现某个系统只有一个人懂的情况。
text_es: Entonces necesitas que se despeguen de las otras cosas en las que están trabajando. Si ves el panorama general, digamos la vista desde arriba sin perderte en los detalles, lo que quieres es que la gente trabaje en parejas y que vayan rotando para que nadie sea el único dueño del sistema.
key_sentence: Shed their skin to avoid being single owners of the system.
original_text: So you need to shed their skin of the other things that they're working on. If you take a bigger picture, kind of forest through the trees picture, you want people pairing and switching pairs so they're not single owners of the system. So when they have an opportunity to do something that could be really important to the company beyond one of these isolated teams, they can fade out and not be the only owner that has to transfer knowledge and then field questions for two years on how that system works.

vocabulary.definition: The bigger picture refers to the overall perspective or context of a situation, encompassing all relevant factors and implications beyond immediate details.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business strategy discussions, focusing on the bigger picture helps teams align their efforts with long-term goals and understand how individual tasks contribute to broader objectives.
vocabulary.nuance: While emphasizing the bigger picture is important for strategic thinking, it can sometimes lead to overlooking critical details that require attention.

vocabulary.definition: Single owners refer to individuals who are solely responsible for a specific system, project, or area of expertise within an organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup settings, having single owners can lead to knowledge silos, where critical information is concentrated in one person, potentially creating risks if that individual becomes unavailable.
vocabulary.nuance: While single ownership can promote accountability, it is often advisable to encourage shared ownership to foster collaboration and mitigate risks associated with dependency on one individual.
